\section[eṅṅane]{\ml{എങ്ങനെ} (eṅṅane) — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} another of the e- questions}

\label{lesson:ML-C03-engane}



\begin{quote}
You met \textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}} (\emph{entŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) in Chapter 2. Here is its sibling in Malayalam's question family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Malayalam.)} \textbf{\ml{എ}} (independent \emph{e}) + \textbf{\ml{ങ്ങ}} (\emph{ṅṅa}, a doubled velar nasal) + \textbf{\ml{നെ}} (\emph{ne}) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{എങ്ങനെ}} (\emph{eṅṅane}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{എങ്ങനെ}} (\emph{eṅṅane}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, on the interrogative base \textbf{e-} you met in \emph{entŭ}. Malayalam gathers its questions here: \emph{entŭ} (what), \emph{eṅṅane} (how), \emph{ārŭ} (who), \emph{eviṭe} (where), \emph{eppōḷ} (when), \emph{entinŭ} (why). It is the same Dravidian question-root heading Tamil's \emph{eppaḍi} — the deepest, most native layer of a language otherwise rich in Sanskrit.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}eṅṅane\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the e- question family — \emph{entŭ, eṅṅane, ārŭ, eviṭe, eppōḷ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nī / niṅṅaḷ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What base do Malayalam's question-words share, and which Tamil cousin heads its own? (The interrogative \emph{e-}; Tamil's \emph{eppaḍi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ō]{\ml{ഓ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S126-letter-oo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ൺ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഓ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഓ}} — \emph{ō}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape this vowel takes when a word \emph{begins} with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

You copied its other half in the last chapter. Inside \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} the vowel \emph{ō} is a \textbf{sign} wrapped around its consonant: \textbf{\ml{◌ോ}}. Where the vowel has no consonant to wrap around, it stands up as a letter of its own: \textbf{\ml{ഓ}}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} \emph{santōṣam} — the sign form, already in your hand
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഓ}} — the letter form, which arrives on the next page as the ending that turns a Malayalam statement into a question
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ഓ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{ഓ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}

That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\end{quote}

\section[sukhamāṇō?]{\ml{സുഖമാണോ}? (sukhamāṇō?) — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C03-sukhamaano}



\begin{quote}
Malayalam usually asks after your health rather than \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{} — and the question is built from a Chapter-2 word plus a single new sound.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} (\emph{sukhaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}well-being\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} (\emph{āṇŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} from Chapter 2) + the question-marker \textbf{\ml{ഓ}} (\emph{ō}) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണോ}} (\emph{sukhamāṇō}), \textquotedblleft{}is {[}it{]} well?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണോ}?} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{is {[}it{]} well?}\textquotedblright{} — where English says \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}, Malayalam more often says \textquotedblleft{}are you well?\textquotedblright{} The word \textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} (\emph{sukhaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}well-being, comfort, ease\textquotedblright{}) is a \textbf{Sanskrit} loan — \emph{sukha} itself, borrowed whole (the \emph{su-} \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} that is Greek \emph{eu-}). Onto it, Malayalam adds its own \textbf{native copula} \emph{āṇŭ} (\textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} from Chapter 2) and the question particle \textbf{-ō} — a whole yes/no question made by one small sound at the end. This mix — a Sanskrit noun, a Dravidian verb — is Malayalam in miniature.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: turning a statement into a question}]
Malayalam makes a yes/no question by adding \textbf{-ō} to the end: \emph{sukham āṇŭ} (\textquotedblleft{}it is well\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{sukham āṇō?} (\textquotedblleft{}is it well?\textquotedblright{}). No change of word order, no helper — just the little \emph{-ō}. You will use it to question any statement.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sukhamāṇō?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Sanskrit word for well-being inside it (\emph{sukha})
  \item how Malayalam makes a yes/no question (add \emph{-ō})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sukhamāṇō?} literally ask, and what are its Sanskrit and Dravidian pieces? (\textquotedblleft{}Is {[}it{]} well?\textquotedblright{}; Sanskrit \emph{sukha} \textquotedblleft{}well-being\textquotedblright{} + the native copula \emph{āṇŭ} + the question \emph{-ō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\ml{◌െ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S139-vowel-sign-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ഓ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌െ}}
\textbf{\ml{◌െ}} — \emph{e}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{e}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You have been reading this one since the first chapter without being told its name.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{അതെ}} \emph{athe} — yes
  \item \textbf{\ml{എന്റെ}} \emph{enṟe} — my
\end{itemize}

It is the short partner of \textbf{\ml{◌േ}}, the long sign in \textbf{\ml{പേര്}}. Both stand to the LEFT of the consonant they belong to and are pronounced AFTER it, so in \textbf{\ml{അതെ}} the hook belongs to the \textbf{\ml{ത}} on its right: \emph{ta} $\to$ \emph{te}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{◌െ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{◌െ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{◌െ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}

\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[ñān]{\ml{ഞാൻ} (ñān) — \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the Dravidian first person}

\label{lesson:ML-C03-njaan}



\begin{quote}
To answer, you first need \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — and it opens with a sound English never starts a word with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{ഞ}} (\emph{ña} — a palatal nasal, like the \textquotedblleft{}ny\textquotedblright{} in \emph{canyon}, but at the very start of the word) + \textbf{\ml{ാ}} (long \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\ml{ൻ}} (the special word-final \emph{n}, called \emph{chillŭ}) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} (\emph{ñān}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} (\emph{ñān}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*yāṉ / *ñāṉ} — native, and (unlike Hindi's \emph{maiṁ}, cousin of English \emph{me}) \textbf{not} related to the European \textquotedblleft{}I/me\textquotedblright{} family. Its possessive is the \textbf{\ml{എന്റെ}} (\emph{enṟe}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) you already met: \emph{ñān} \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} \emph{enṟe} \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{} Malayalam layered a great deal of Sanskrit over its vocabulary, but the pronoun for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} is bedrock Dravidian.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Malayalam does \emph{not} drop \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}}]
Here Malayalam parts from its sisters. Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu verbs carry the person in their ending, so they freely drop \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} But \textbf{Malayalam verbs do not change for person at all} (you'll see this in Chapter 5) — so the pronoun \emph{ñān} must be said. It cannot be left out, because the verb won't tell you who acts.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ñān\textquotedblright{} — start with the \textquotedblleft{}ny\textquotedblright{} sound
  \item \emph{Say it:} the pair — \emph{ñān} (I), \emph{enṟe} (my)
  \item \emph{Say it:} can Malayalam drop \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} like Tamil? (No — its verbs don't mark person)
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{ñān}'s possessive, and why must Malayalam say \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} where Tamil can drop it? (\emph{Enṟe}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}; Malayalam verbs don't change for person, so the pronoun is needed.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sukhaṁ]{\ml{സുഖം} (sukhaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}well-being,\textquotedblright{} and how to answer}

\label{lesson:ML-C03-sukham}



\begin{quote}
The word at the heart of \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and it travelled all the way from Sanskrit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{സു}} (\emph{su}) + \textbf{\ml{ഖം}} (\emph{khaṁ}, an aspirated \emph{kh} + the \emph{anusvāra}) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} (\emph{sukhaṁ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} (\emph{sukhaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}well-being, comfort, ease, happiness\textquotedblright{}) is a \textbf{Sanskrit} loan — \emph{sukha} = \emph{su-} (\textquotedblleft{}good, well\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{kha} (\textquotedblleft{}space, feeling\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{su-} that is Greek \emph{eu-} (as in \emph{euphoria}). Malayalam, Tamil's closest sister, took far more Sanskrit into everyday speech than Tamil did — and \emph{sukham} is a perfect case: for \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} where Tamil answers with native \emph{nalam}, Malayalam reaches for Sanskrit \emph{sukham}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{The exchange — the reply}
With the copula from Chapter 2: \textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണ്}} (\emph{sukhamāṇŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}I am{]} well}\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}{[}it{]} is well\textquotedblright{}). The whole exchange:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{sukhamāṇō?} (\textquotedblleft{}Are you well? / How are you?\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{sukhamāṇŭ, nandi.} (\textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

Notice the reply reuses the greeting's own words — \emph{sukham} + \emph{āṇŭ} — just without the question \emph{-ō}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sukhaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the full reply — \emph{sukhamāṇŭ, nandi}
  \item the Sanskrit root and its Greek twin (\emph{su-} = Greek \emph{eu-})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the reply to \emph{sukhamāṇō?}, and say where \emph{sukham} comes from. (\emph{Sukhamāṇŭ}; Sanskrit \emph{sukha}, \textquotedblleft{}well-being\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{su-} that is Greek \emph{eu-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[sāramilla]{\ml{സാരമില്ല} (sāramilla) — \textquotedblleft{}it doesn't matter\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C03-saaramilla}



\begin{quote}
When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply, and it fuses Malayalam's two heritages in one word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{സാരം}} (\emph{sāraṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}substance, matter\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} (\emph{illa}, \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സാരമില്ല}} (\emph{sāramilla}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{സാരമില്ല}} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{there's no matter to it / it doesn't matter}\textquotedblright{} — used for \textquotedblleft{}never mind / no worries / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} It is a perfect little emblem of Malayalam: \textbf{\ml{സാരം}} (\emph{sāraṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}substance, essence\textquotedblright{}) is a \textbf{Sanskrit} loan, while \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} (\emph{illa}, \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}) is the \textbf{native Dravidian} negative from Chapter 1. Sanskrit noun, Dravidian verb, welded into one everyday word. That \emph{illa} is the same \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{} shared across \textbf{Malayalam, Tamil, and Kannada} — one of the deep bonds of the south (Telugu alone diverges, to \emph{lēdu}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \ml{ഇല്ല}, the all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}]
\emph{Illa} negates existence and stands alone as \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}: \emph{paṇam illa} (\textquotedblleft{}there's no money\textquotedblright{}), \emph{ñān illa} (\textquotedblleft{}it's not me / I'm not {[}there{]}\textquotedblright{}). It is the negative twin of the copula \emph{āṇŭ} (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) you learned in Chapter 2 — \emph{āṇŭ} affirms, \emph{illa} denies.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sāramilla\textquotedblright{}
  \item its two heritages (Sanskrit \emph{sāraṁ} + native \emph{illa})
  \item the \emph{āṇŭ} / \emph{illa} pair — \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sāramilla} literally say, and which of its two words is Sanskrit? (\textquotedblleft{}There's no matter / it doesn't matter\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sāraṁ} \textquotedblleft{}substance\textquotedblright{} is Sanskrit, \emph{illa} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} is native Dravidian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 3 — The how-are-you exchange}

\label{lesson:ML-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole responding cycle, from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Are you well? / How are you?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sukhamāṇō?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sukhamāṇŭ, nandi.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}It doesn't matter / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sāramilla.}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the e- question-word for \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} (\emph{eṅṅane})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — and why Malayalam can't drop it (\emph{ñān}; its verbs don't mark person)
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}is / is-not\textquotedblright{} pair (\emph{āṇŭ} / \emph{illa})
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eṅṅane} $\leftarrow$ the interrogative \emph{e-} (native Dravidian, like Tamil \emph{eppaḍi})
  \item \emph{ñān} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian (unrelated to English \emph{me}); possessive \emph{enṟe}
  \item \emph{sukham} $\leftarrow$ \textbf{Sanskrit} \emph{sukha} \textquotedblleft{}well-being\textquotedblright{} (the \emph{su-} that is Greek \emph{eu-})
  \item \emph{āṇŭ} / \emph{illa} — \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{}; \emph{illa} shared with Tamil \& Kannada
  \item the question-marker \emph{-ō} — turns any statement into a yes/no question
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Script check — the letters of this chapter}
Cover the romanizations. Find each letter once in the Malayalam above, then say the word it sits in.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ആണോ}?} — \textbf{\ml{ഓ}} \emph{ō}, the question ending, standing as its own letter
  \item \textbf{\ml{അതെ}}, \textbf{\ml{എന്റെ}} — \textbf{\ml{◌െ}} \emph{e}
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} — \textbf{\ml{ഇ}} \emph{i}
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at each letter, then find it in the word beside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A friend asks \emph{sukhamāṇō?} — give a full, polite reply, and answer their thanks. (\emph{Sukhamāṇŭ, nandi} — and to thanks, \emph{sāramilla}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[santōṣam]{\ml{സന്തോഷം} — one delayed copy}

\label{lesson:ML-W03-santosham-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Look at \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} for five seconds and say \emph{santōṣam}. Find \textbf{\ml{ഷ}} and the long \emph{ō} sign \textbf{\ml{ോ}} once more. Then cover the model with your hand or a small piece of paper.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — one try after a delay}
Write \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} once while the model is covered. This is a gentle retrieval, not a speed test. If one shape will not come, uncover the model, look, cover it again, and finish.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Uncover \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}} and compare it with your copy. Repair only one shape if needed. Say \emph{santōṣam} once, then stop: one known word, one spaced writing revisit.
\end{tcolorbox}
